title: Vex Lesson
cardBrief: Theo drills Meilin until the crossbow becomes procedure, not performance. She learns to strike when attention is split: exploit the flinch, hit when the target is already compromised.
keyTakeaways: **Method over heroics**: Theo sets a target and refuses to call it training; he calls it repetition.
**Muscle memory**: Meilin drills the hand crossbow until the motion becomes procedure.
**Exploit the flinch**: Theo teaches her the real point: hit to steal a moment, then exploit the blink.
**Tactical patience**: She learns to wait for split attention and wrong footing, not for "fair."
**Live application**: Days later, a crowd incident gives her a live test of that lesson.
**Precision in chaos**: She fires when the real actor commits, then cuts a runner free before the scene turns lethal.
content:
Theo Lockwell doesn’t call it training.

He calls it **repetition**.

Meilin stands in a narrow alley behind his shop where the Bazaar’s noise turns into a constant hiss. Someone has painted a target circle on a board that used to be a crate lid. The paint is old enough to have given up on perfection.

Theo sets a compact crossbow on the bench like it’s a tool, not a statement.

“It’s not a duelist’s weapon,” he says. “It’s for people who don’t get second chances.”

Meilin doesn’t argue. She checks the string. Checks the notch. Checks the bolt seating. Her fingers move in the same pattern she uses when laying out bandage, needle, tincture: everything in reach, everything where it belongs.

“You don’t shoot to be brave,” Theo continues. “You shoot to make the next moment easier.”

Meilin raises the weapon.

The first bolt goes wide.

Theo doesn’t laugh. He just nods like he expected that outcome.

“Again,” he says.

Meilin breathes out, slow, and shoots again.

This time the bolt strikes the board with a blunt, satisfying thunk. Not center. Not perfect. But **true**.

Theo says, “Good. Now do it the way it matters.”

He steps into Meilin’s peripheral vision (not blocking the shot, just *present*).

Meilin’s hands tighten.

“You see?” Theo says. “The Bazaar never gives you a clean lane. People move. They shout. Someone’s always in the way.”

Meilin doesn’t lower the crossbow. She does what she does when a patient starts panicking: narrows her attention to the useful variables.

Angle. Risk. Breath.

Then she fires.

The bolt strikes the board again.

Theo’s mouth twitches. “Now you’re learning.”

Meilin frowns. “That wasn’t different.”

Theo taps the board with a knuckle. “It was. You didn’t chase precision. You chased **control**.”

He walks behind her and speaks close to her ear, not threatening, just teaching.

“When you land a hit, you steal a moment from them,” he says. “Pain makes people blink. Anger makes them look at the wrong thing. That blink is your opening.”

Meilin’s eyes flick to the bolt sunk in the wood. A new kind of ledger entry.

Cause. Effect.

Theo slides another bolt into her reach. “Put the next one where it belongs.”

Meilin raises the crossbow again.

She doesn’t aim with romance.

She aims with math.

The bolt strikes the board a handspan from the first. Close enough to prove intent. Close enough to say: **I can repeat this.**

Theo nods once. “That’s the point. Not the first hit. The second.”

Meilin’s pulse steadies.

She can feel the shape of it now: hit, then exploit the flinch, the way a system shows you its weakness the moment you apply pressure.

She doesn’t call it mastery.

She calls it **practice until it becomes procedure**.

---

The Bazaar tests her lesson within days.

It isn’t a dramatic fight. It’s the kind of problem that grows from crowds: a vendor screaming, a customer claiming theft, a guard stepping in with the bored cruelty of someone who’d rather punish than understand.

The accused is a young runner (thin, scared, and too proud to beg). Their wrists are bound with cord tight enough to leave pale lines.

Meilin doesn’t care about the shouting.

She cares about the hands.

She moves like she belongs there, because looking lost is the fastest way to become prey. The crowd tightens. The guard barks something about “order.”

Then someone in the back shifts.

Not toward the guard.

Toward the bound runner.

Meilin sees it the way she sees contamination: the wrong movement in the wrong place. A second actor. A follow-up. The real theft about to happen while everyone watches the loud part.

The runner flinches as the hidden figure closes in (half protection, half opportunism). Meilin can’t tell.

It doesn’t matter yet.

Meilin’s hand crossbow comes up under her cloak line, compact and unheroic.

She waits.

Not because she’s afraid.

Because she’s disciplined.

The guard is still yelling. The crowd is still staring. The hidden figure’s attention is split: on the runner’s pocket, on the guard’s distraction, on their own exit.

Meilin fires.

The bolt hits meat, not bone, high in the shoulder, a place that makes a person drop what they’re doing and turn toward the pain.

The figure staggers, surprised into honesty.

In that same heartbeat, the guard’s attention snaps away from the runner.

The crowd breaks its shape.

Meilin doesn’t take a victory lap.

She steps in close, fast, and cuts the runner’s cord with a blade that looks like an apothecary’s tool because it *is* an apothecary’s tool.

“Move,” she says quietly, not kind, not cruel, clinical.

The runner bolts into the crowd like they’ve been waiting for permission to live.

Behind them, the wounded figure tries to stand their ground, eyes wild with rage.

Meilin doesn’t give them a speech.

She simply re-aims while their attention is still broken, while their stance is still wrong, while their mind is still catching up to pain.

And she understands, with the cold clarity of a diagnosis:

The hit isn’t the trick.

The trick is choosing the moment when the target can’t afford to fully notice her.

That’s how she survives the Bazaar.

Not by fighting fair.

By fighting **when the system is already distracted**.
